payload.text: Honestly? The math was the easy part.
Then you put four pieces of glass in a cavity... and a few microns is suddenly your whole afternoon.
The first version technically worked. And by 'worked,' I mean... if you didn't breathe near it. [laughs]
This mirror mount took me three days. Before the pre-seed, half of this was 3D-printed. [short pause] Now it's, like... a third.
There was this night the camera image finally matched what the simulator said it should look like. And we just... stared at it for a while.
Getting from that to something you can turn on, calibrate, and run again tomorrow... that was most of the engineering.
I didn't care that it was optical. I cared that it was fast.
Once the machine worked, the question changed. Not: can light compute? But: what happens when it does?
Every pass through the cavity is one recurrent step. Which is beautiful, mathematically. But it also means every tiny error gets another chance to matter.
They ran the same workload, and I honestly thought the dashboard was broken.
We used to treat inference like a budget. How many times can we afford to call the model? Now the conversation is: how often do we want to?
I was like... [laughs] wait, that's our energy bill? That number's supposed to have another digit.
After a week, waiting two hundred milliseconds felt broken.
The strange thing about computing at this scale is that, eventually, the software problem becomes a power problem.
You start arguing about transformers.
PHASER changes the slope of that curve.
If every new unit of intelligence needs its own block of electricity, the bottleneck stops being algorithms.
Energy isn't an AI resource.
It's a civilization resource.
It moves water.
It runs hospitals.
It grows, cools and carries food.
It heats homes.
It builds things.
And increasingly, it runs intelligence.
PHASER doesn't make energy unimportant.
It makes computation ask for less of it.
The question isn't whether we want more intelligence. We do. The question is what it has to consume.
We built PHASER so that more intelligence doesn't have to mean more heat.

payload.text: So we built one that computes with light.
Every computer you've ever used works the same way. It pushes electrons through metal... and most of that energy just turns into heat.
Then you put four pieces of glass in a cavity... and a few microns is suddenly your whole afternoon.
Honestly? The math was the easy part.
Before the pre-seed, half of this was 3D-printed. [short pause] Now it's, like... a third.
She made us run it again. [laughs] Then she asked if that was really the energy number.

The first time a customer ran their real workload on it, their head of infrastructure thought the dashboard was broken.
You end up arguing about transformers.
If every new unit of intelligence needs its own block of electricity, the bottleneck stops being algorithms.
PHASER changes the slope of that curve.
Energy isn't an AI resource. [short pause] It's a civilization resource.
It runs hospitals.
It moves water.
It heats homes.
And increasingly, it runs intelligence.
It builds things.
The question isn't whether we want more intelligence. We do. The question is what it has to consume.
PHASER doesn't make energy unimportant.
It makes computation ask for less of it.
We taught light to compute.
It grows, cools and carries food.
The first version technically worked. And by 'worked,' I mean... if you didn't breathe near it. [laughs]
The strange thing about AI at this scale is that, eventually, the software problem becomes a power problem.
That's when the question changes. Not: can light compute? But: what happens when it does?
